stories.headline: APRIL PAYROLLS CRUSH ESTIMATES: 115K JOBS ADDED VS. 62K FORECAST
stories.body: The U.S. economy added 115,000 jobs in April — nearly double the 62K consensus — while March was revised up to 185K. Wage growth softened to 3.6% YoY (vs. 3.8% expected), moderating the bond selloff. S&P 500 futures surged on the release, and both the index and Nasdaq are on pace for a sixth consecutive weekly gain — the longest winning streak since October 2024.

stories.headline: IRAN AND US TRADE FRESH BLOWS AS CEASEFIRE MOU TALKS REMAIN UNFINISHED
stories.body: Iranian forces struck a U.S. destroyer transiting the Strait of Hormuz Thursday; Trump threatened harder strikes unless a deal closes quickly. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are negotiating a 14-point memorandum of understanding — including a nuclear enrichment moratorium, partial sanctions relief, and Hormuz reopening — but gaps on ballistic missiles and regional proxies persist. Polymarket prices a 23.5% chance of a comprehensive deal by May 31.

stories.headline: S&P 500 POSTS FRESH RECORD AT 7,392, NASDAQ +0.66%, SIXTH STRAIGHT WINNING WEEK
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.41% to 7,392 and the Nasdaq gained 0.66% to 26,200, both hitting all-time highs. The Russell 2000 added 0.49% to 2,854. Equities are navigating a dual tailwind of labor market resilience and Iran deal optionality, while $95 WTI and rising hike odds represent the key risk-off threats to the rally.

stories.headline: WARSH'S FIRST DATA TEST: HOT JOBS CEMENTS 'HIGHER FOR LONGER,' HIKE ODDS HIT 38.5%
stories.body: April's payroll beat is the first major macro print under incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who inherits a 3.5–3.75% policy rate and a committee with four dissents at Powell's final April 29 meeting. CME FedWatch prices a near-90% probability of no cut through year-end, while the chance of at least one hike over the next 12 months has climbed to 38.5%. Goldman Sachs expects the easing bias to be dropped at Warsh's June 17–18 debut meeting.

stories.headline: OIL RISK PREMIUM HOLDS: WTI $95.46, BRENT $100.54 DESPITE CEASEFIRE HOPE
stories.body: WTI crude rose 0.69% to $95.46/bbl and Brent gained 0.48% to $100.54/bbl, recouping some of Wednesday's Iran-deal-driven crash. Both benchmarks remain roughly 50% above pre-conflict levels, adding an estimated 0.4–0.5 percentage points annually to headline CPI. Gold rose 0.43% to $4,706/oz — up 42% year-over-year — as dollar weakness and inflation hedging sustain bullion demand.

stories.headline: MARCH MADNESS EXPANDING TO 76 TEAMS STARTING 2027 AFTER NCAA VOTE
stories.body: The NCAA voted to expand both the men's and women's Division I basketball tournaments from 68 to 76 teams beginning in 2027. The new format introduces an 'Opening Round' of 12 games across two days before the traditional First Round, unlocking over $131 million in additional revenue distributions to member schools over the remaining six years of the broadcast deal. Michigan won the 2026 title; the 76-team era begins next March.

stories.headline: WEMBANYAMA SHATTERS PLAYOFF BLOCKS RECORD WITH 12 IN SPURS-WOLVES SEMIS GAME 1
stories.body: Victor Wembanyama recorded 12 blocked shots in San Antonio's Conference Semifinals Game 1 against Minnesota — a single-game NBA playoff record. In the East, Detroit holds a 2-0 series lead over Cleveland after Thursday's 107-97 win: Cade Cunningham posted 25 points and 10 assists, and the top-seeded Pistons have won both games by double digits. Game 3 moves to Cleveland on Saturday.

stories.headline: NFL LOCKS IN MAY 14 SCHEDULE RELEASE AS ALL 32 TEAMS FINALIZE DEPTH CHARTS
stories.body: The league confirmed the 2026 NFL schedule will be released Thursday, May 14 at 8 PM ET on NFL Network and ESPN2. Teams continue offseason work: the Seahawks are in Phase 2 OTAs with the youngest roster in the NFC West, having added DE Dante Fowler and TE Harrison Bryant post-draft. Seattle's Week 1 opponent — Sept. 9 on NBC — remains unannounced pending the release.

stories.headline: PROGRAMS FINALIZE 2026 ROSTERS AS JANUARY-ONLY PORTAL WINDOW RESHAPES OFFSEASON
stories.body: With the NCAA's new single January transfer window closed, teams are completing rosters through existing commitments. Washington's schedule gained two Friday prime-time windows: the Huskies will host Iowa on Oct. 9 and visit Purdue on Oct. 16, per a Big Ten/FOX Sports announcement today. Post-spring national rankings have Texas atop most polls with Arch Manning healthy, while Notre Dame's Blue-Gold Game drew 45,308 — the second-largest spring game crowd in program history.

deepDive.title: Kevin Warsh Takes the Wheel — What the Fed Chair Succession Means for Rates in 2026
content: Kevin Warsh officially succeeds Jerome Powell as Federal Reserve Chair this month, inheriting an economy that is simultaneously too hot to cut and too uncertain to hike. Today's April jobs report — 115,000 payrolls against a 62,000 consensus — is his first major macroeconomic data test. He walks into a 3.5–3.75% policy rate, a committee where four members dissented at Powell's April 29 farewell meeting (the most since 1992), oil at $95/bbl adding an estimated half-point to CPI, and market-implied hike odds at 38.5%. The June 17–18 FOMC is already positioned as the most consequential meeting in years.

Warsh's policy philosophy differs from Powell's data-driven gradualism in three meaningful ways. First, he is explicitly 'market-aware' — during his 2006–2011 tenure as a Fed governor, he argued that asset prices contain forward-looking signals the Fed should incorporate, not just lag traditional models. Second, he is institutionally hawkish on inflation credibility: he publicly opposed QE3 in 2012, arguing the Fed's credibility is its most valuable long-run asset, worth short-term pain to defend. Third, expect tighter policy language and a higher bar for forward guidance — Warsh has written that the Fed signals too often and too loosely, and he will likely tighten the committee's communication discipline from day one.

The four dissents at April's FOMC — three governors pushing to drop forward-guidance language, one calling for an immediate cut — signal that Warsh is inheriting a fractured committee, not a consensus-building exercise. This matters because a divided Fed amplifies statement-language volatility: markets cannot price policy risk off a single chair's guidance when the committee itself disagrees. The most instructive historical parallel is Arthur Burns (1970), who inherited a tight labor market, faced stagflationary oil shocks, and repeatedly capitulated to political pressure. Warsh has explicitly cited Burns as the cautionary tale modern Fed chairs must avoid — his credibility as a hawk may be tested as early as this summer.

The June meeting setup is the critical tell. With April wages at 3.6% YoY (below the 3.8% expected), Warsh has cover to hold without explicitly signaling hikes — the 'soft wages, hot headline' combination gives the committee optionality in both directions. The real signal will be statement language: removing the 'easing bias' (the clause that leans toward future cuts) would reanchor expectations without committing to tightening. If the statement is unchanged from April, markets will read it as dovish by omission. Fed funds futures currently price the first potential cut no earlier than Q4 2027 — a dramatic reversal from early 2026's hopes for summer easing.
